list.listitem: Suspect cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients with persistent skin rash in the form of patches, plaques, or erythroderma, which may be localized or widespread. Patients frequently have been previously (incorrectly) diagnosed with eczema or psoriasis.C

When CTCL is suspected, perform a skin biopsy, order labs, and consider referral to a specialist for assistance with diagnosis and further workup. Multiple biopsies may be needed over time to establish the diagnosis as it takes a median of 4 years from rash onset to diagnosis.C
Labs should include a complete blood count, blood smear to evaluate for Sézary cells, comprehensive metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase, and flow cytometry. C
There is no cure for CTCL, hence the approach should be palliative and follow a stepwise stage-adjusted method. C

Very early-stage mycosis fungoides (MF) typically has an indolent course with slow progression over years and a normal life expectancy, while Sézary syndrome (SS) has a less favorable prognosis with median survival between 1 to 4 years.B

background.definition: Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) are a subgroup of non-Hodgkin lymphomas where T-lymphocytes proliferate in the skin and other involved organs. The most common type of CTCL is mycosis fungoides (MF). Sézary syndrome (SS) is differentiated from MF by evidence of leukemic involvement. This topic focuses on these subtypes with some mention of the primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders. There are other rarer types of CTCL that are very aggressive and are managed differently than the CTCLs presented here.

list.listitem: Incidence of primary cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCLs) is 0.6 /100,000 persons/year.

The most common type of CTCL is mycosis fungoides (MF), making up approximately 50% of all cutaneous lymphomas. The primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma and lymphomatoid papulosis) account for 30%, while Sézary syndrome (SS) makes up only 3% to 4% of cases.
MF typically affects older adults with a median age at diagnosis of 55 to 60 years but may also occur in children. SS only occurs in adults.
Mycosis fungoides is 1.6 to 2 times more common in men than in women.
Although a number of theories have been proposed as causative agents, including chemical and viral exposures, none have been confirmed.

A single centre retrospective cohort study of breast implant associated anaplastic large cell NHL suggests a possible link of textured breast implants to T cell lymphoma more than 10 years later at this site, with a number needed to treat to harm of 559.

It is proposed that immune modulating antibody therapy may be a trigger for cutaneous T cell lymphoma. In a retrospective cohort treated with duplimab for atopic dermatitis the odds ratio for subsequent development of CTCL was 4.0, although this may not be a causal link.
Mycosis fungoides (MF) and Sézary syndrome (SS) cells are typically CD4+/CD8- helper T-cells in the skin and other involved organs.

SS is a leukemic version of CTCL and is characterized by cerebriform cells, called Sézary cells, circulating in the blood. On flow cytometry of blood, >30% of lymphocytes are CD4+/CD7- and/or 40% are CD4+/CD26.

The primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoproliferative disorders, primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, and lymphomatoid papulosis are characterized by large CD30+ T-cells. MF can sometimes express small amounts of CD30.
There are no recommended screening tests or preventive strategies for CTCL. C
Suspect cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients with persistent skin rash in the form of patches, plaques, or erythroderma, with or without lymphadenopathy and organomegaly. C

When CTCL is suspected, perform skin biopsy and order labs including a complete blood count, blood smear to evaluate for Sézary cells, comprehensive metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase, and flow cytometry. C
Consider referral for lymph-node biopsy, if accessible. Multiple skin biopsies may be needed over time to establish the diagnosis. C

Erythematous patches with scale, often well demarcated
Pruritic erythematous patches and plaques, often with scale
Erythematous patches with scale, often well demarcated
Pruritic and often painful erythematous pustules and papules on hair-bearing areas
Erythematous maculopapular rash or well circumscribed pruritic wheals
Pruritic thin white papules and plaques

list.listitem: The International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL)/European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) guidelines for diagnosis of early mycosis fungoides (MF) are based on the following criteria: 1) clinical, 2) histopathologic, 3) molecular biologic (T-cell clonality), and 4) immunopathologic features.

International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL)/European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) guidelines for staging MF and SS use a TNMB system, which includes the following four criteria: clinical appearance and extent of the skin involvement (T), clinical and histologic evaluation of abnormal peripheral lymph nodes (N), involvement of visceral organs determined by imaging (M), and blood involvement including percent of Sézary cells (B).
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL), particularly mycosis fungoides (MF), is often referred to as the great imitator, as the rash may take on many different appearances.

The classic presentation is a patch or plaque that is persistent or progressive in a non-sun exposed area. Most are large (>5 cm diameter) and have poikiloderma, characterized by mottled pigmentation, telangiectasia, and cigarette-paper wrinkling with some slight infiltration.
The rash of CTCL typically either incompletely clears with topical corticosteroids or recurs when therapy is discontinued.
In a retrospective analysis, pruritus was present in 66% of patients with MF or Sézary syndrome (SS).
Other possible characteristics of lesions of CTCL include papules, hypopigmented or hyperpigmented lesions, generalized erythroderma, skin tumors, alopecia, bulla, and vesicles.

A systematic review of case series found that the most common features seen in mycosis fungoides orange-yellow patches, fine short linear vessels/linear vessels, and squiggly spermatozoa-like vessels.

Diagnosis is made with skin biopsies that include evaluation with dermatopathology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular analysis. Consider evaluation by a dermatopathologist experienced in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL).
A broad shave biopsy, including a wide area of the dermoepidermal junction, is preferred to increase diagnostic yield, but a punch biopsy also may be sufficient.
Topical steroids and systemic immunosuppressants may affect biopsy results for 2 to 4 weeks, so ideally should be held prior to biopsy.

Mycosis fungoides (MF) can be diagnosed based on a skin biopsy with typical features, but early MF may be difficult to determine by biopsy alone as features on biopsy may mimic cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia (ie, reactions to arthropod bites, tattoos, etc.), pityriasis lichenoides, hypereosinophilic syndrome, histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis, traumatic ulcerative granuloma, or pigmented purpuric dermatosis.
Multiple skin biopsies may be necessary to make a definitive diagnosis.
Diagnosis may also be made by blood studies or a lymph-node biopsy if skin biopsy is not diagnostic. Consider biopsy of peripheral lymph nodes if >1.5 cm in diameter.
Initial laboratory evaluation should include a complete blood count, blood smear to evaluate for Sézary cells, comprehensive metabolic panel, lactate dehydrogenase, and flow cytometry.

Genetic testing such as T-cell receptor (TCR) PCR or high-throughput sequencing can be considered with specialist guidance. The findings of the same T-cell clone in multiple biopsy sites or in skin and blood can help to confirm the diagnosis. High-throughput sequencing, although not readily available, may be more specific and sensitive than TCR PCR in studies. One study showed genetic testing through high-throughput sequencing can be performed and is more specific than T-cell receptor gamma chain gene (TRG) PCR and flow cytometry but equally sensitive and accurate, while another showed high-throughput TCR sequencing (HTS) was more sensitive and specific than TCR PCR and can successfully discriminate CTCL from benign inflammatory diseases. Future genetic studies may include biomarkers and microRNA profiling to differentiate Sézary syndrome (SS) from other erythrodermic inflammatory dermatitis, such as psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.

The molecular markers T-plastin, Twist and KIR3DL2 were best at distinguishing mycosis fungoides from Sezary syndrome, with higher values of each bioimarker in patients with Sezary syndrome in a cohort of 447 patients. The optimal cutoffs were > 53.2 for T-plastin (46% sensitive and 95% specific), > 68.4 for Twist (53% sensitive and 93% specific), and > 154.9 for KIR3DL2 (50% sensitive and 95% specific).Table 365

The need for imaging depends on the extent of organ involvement and should be determined with specialist guidance. In patients with limited skin involvement (<10%) and without palpably enlarged nodes who are otherwise healthy and without complaints consistent with organ involvement, a chest x-ray and ultrasound of peripheral lymph-node groups may suffice, though many experts will obtain further imaging.

CT scan of the chest, abdomen, pelvis, +/- PET scan are recommended for patients with Sézary syndrome, more extensive skin or nodal involvement by MF, or with one of the CD30+ primary cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorders. PET scan has a low sensitivity in detecting primary CTCL but may be more sensitive than CT at detecting distant metastases and can be helpful in staging.

Suspect cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) in patients with a persistent rash. Characteristics of the rash may vary but clinicians should have a high degree of suspicion in patients with patches, plaques, or erythroderma, and in patients with swollen lymph nodes.

If initial biopsy is unrevealing, another biopsy may be warranted. Laboratory studies as described above may be obtained at time of biopsy. Referral to specialist care to determine further workup including biopsies and radiologic studies should then occur.
See and for ISCL/EORTC clinical staging.
Early-stage disease (Stage I-IIA) includes patients with less than 80% skin involvement, no skin tumors, minimal or no blood involvement, and minimal nodal involvement.

Treatment of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL) involves a multidisciplinary team consisting of primary care, hematology/oncology, dermatology, wound care, and possibly radiation oncology, according to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) Guidelines. C

There are only a limited number of randomized studies to guide treatment of mycosis fungoides (MF) or Sézary syndrome (SS) and most treatment is determined by expert opinion and varies by institution. C

There is no cure for CTCL, hence the approach should be palliative and follow a stepwise stage-adjusted method. Complete remission of disease is extremely rare, so decisions about continuing with the same treatment versus changing to another are individualized, often depending on how satisfied the patient is with the current disease control, such as rash and pruritus.C

According to NCCN guidelines and expert opinion, patients often receive treatment for years, so balancing symptom control with toxicity is an important consideration. Therefore, one drug at a time, rather than multi-agent chemotherapy regimens, is typically used. It may take 3 or more months for a drug to be effective in a patient. Responses are also typically not durable, so frequent changes in medications occur. C
For limited cutaneous involvement, skin-directed therapies may be all that is needed.B

For patients with more extensive skin involvement or for those who cannot be managed with topicals or light therapy, systemic therapy is often required. This is often given in combination with skin-directed therapies, such as topical steroids or light therapy.B

Most patients will remain on indefinite therapy for their mycosis fungoides (MF) or Sézary syndrome (SS). If remission is obtained, it is usually not durable, and patients will usually be on multiple different agents throughout their lives according to the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines.

Primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL) and lymphomatoid papulosis are more likely to be localized to a few spots and may just be treated intermittently with radiation, steroids creams, or surgical resection.

Topical skin-directed therapies may be all that is needed for early-stage disease, but they continue to be an important part of management, even for patients with advanced staging disease receiving systemic therapies.

British Academy of Dermatology guidelines (2018) recommend skin directed therapy including phototherapy and local radiotherapy for patients with early stage (IA - IIA) mycosis fungoides. Patients refractory to skin directed therapy require total skin electron beam therapy (TSEB) and systemic biological therapies. This guideline provides detailed recommendations for therapy.
Topical corticosteroids, such as clobetasol, have a response rate of over 90% in early-stage mycosis fungoides (MF). These are often used long-term on affected areas.

Topical mechlorethamine (HN2) is an alkylating agent used as first-line in stage IA and IIA MF. It should be applied once daily to the affected area. In a randomized controlled multicenter trial comparing HN2 0.02% gel with ointment, the gel had better time-to-response (p < 0.01), although up to 20% of patients withdrew from the study because of drug-related skin irritation.

UV phototherapy, such as PUVA and UVB light, has been widely used for treatment of both MF and SS. It can reduce both lesion size and pruritus. In general, it is useful in plaque-like disease and early stages, but the risks of long-term exposure may increase the risk of melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancers. Light therapy is typically administered multiple times per week and is not available in every dermatologist’s office, so time and travel may be prohibitive for some patients. Light boxes for treatment at home can sometimes be obtained. Light therapy is often used in combination with systemic therapies, such as interferon or retinoids.

For early stage mycosis fungoides the use of topical hypericin combined with light gives a non mutagenic form of photodynamic theapy and a recent placebo controlled trial of this FLASH therapy suggests promising response rates as assessed by response of index lesions.
Local radiation therapy can result in high remission rates and can have durable responses in unilesional disease.

A Cochrane review assessed 20 RCTs (1369 patients) of treatment of CTCL/MF. The conclusion was that there is a lack of high certainty evidence for optimal therapy but that PUVA appears the continuing optimal first line therapy.

BAD guidelines (2018) recommend that patients refractory to skin directed therapy receive total skin electron beam therapy (TSEB) and systemic biological therapies. This guideline provides detailed recommendations for therapy.

Bexarotene, a systemic retinoid, is approved for use in patients with disease refractory to at least one prior systemic therapy. However, in clinical practice it is often used as the initial systemic therapy. In a small randomized trial of 15 patients, oral bexarotene was used for the treatment of refractory or persistent early-stage disease (stage IA and IIA) and showed response rates of about 54%. Triglycerides and thyroid levels should be monitored during treatment.

Methotrexate (MTX) is a well-tolerated single-agent weekly treatment that is also used for MF. There are no prospective clinical trials of single-agent MTX, so its use is largely based on clinical judgement and retrospective studies reporting responses in 33% to 70% of patients.

Interferon-alpha (IFN-alpha) injections 2 to 3 times per week may have both local and systemic effects as evidenced by a small controlled non-randomized study of 22 patients with early- to advanced-stage MF. Fourteen (64%) of the treated patients showed clinical improvement. Side effects include flu-like symptoms, elevated transaminases, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, depression, cardiac arrhythmia, and thyroid dysfunction. Interferons may be combined with retinoids or light therapy. A prospective randomized controlled trial of 98 patients with stage I or II disease, comparing interferon with oral photochemotherapy (PUVA) and interferon with the retinoid acitretin, found a higher rate of complete remission in the interferon/PUVA group than in the interferon/retinoid group (70% vs 38%, p <0.05).
Topical skin-directed therapies listed above in early-stage disease should continue to be used even for patients with advanced-staging disease receiving systemic therapies.

For patients with more widespread disease, total skin electron beam therapy can be very effective. This uses lower doses administered to all areas of the skin for multiple weeks. Often this is combined with localized radiation to individual tumors. Recent studies of few patients demonstrate low-dose schemes show comparable response rates of over 87.5% at 2.5 years. Toxicity is dose-related.

Histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), such as romidepsin or vorinostat, are approved for patients with CTCL who have progressive persistent disease after 1 or 2 (respectively) systemic therapies. Reported response rates are about 30% with toxicities of gastrointestinal side effects, thrombocytopenia, and QTc prolongation.

Chemotherapy may be considered for advanced disease. Single-agent liposomal doxorubicin or gemcitabine are some of the most frequently used. In patients with advanced-stage mycosis fungoides or MF (IIB, IVA, or IVB), 40.8% of patients with refractory or recurrent MF on at least 2 previous systemic therapies had an overall response to liposomal doxorubicin. These were mostly partial responses and the median duration of response was only 6 months in prospective phase II clinical trials. Gemcitabine has shown responses of 62% to 68%, mostly partial responses and, albeit infrequent, can results in long-term remissions in cohort studies

The British Academy of Dermatology guidelines (2018) recommend that patients with stage III erythrodermic mycosis fungoides and patients with stage IVA1 Sezary Syndrome may require single or combination systemic therapies including photopheresis, methotrexate, bexarotene and interferon-alpha as first-line treatment. Alemtezumab is another option for patients with stage IVA1 or 2 Sezary syndrome.
Brentuximab is an option for patients with refractory stage IB disease and advanced stages of MF/SS whose tumour expresses CD30.
Targeted immunotherapy, such as alemtuzumab, brentuximab vedotin, or mogamulizumab, can also be considered for more advanced disease.

Brentuximab vedotin (BV) is an antibody drug conjugate that targets CD30. It is FDA-approved for patients with CD30+ primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, and CD30 expressing MF, that have received at least one prior systemic therapy. A phase III randomized trial compared BV to physician’s choice of oral MTX or bexarotene reported a response lasting at least 4 months in 56% of patients on the BV arm versus 12% of patients on the control arm with a median PFS of 15 months and 4 months, respectively.

Mogamulizumab is a monoclonal antibody-targeting CC chemokine receptor 4 (CCR4), which is expressed on MF cells. A phase III randomized trial compared mogamulizumab to vorinostat in patients with stage IB to IV CTCL after at least one prior therapy. The best overall response was 35% in the mogamulizumab arm with a median PFS of 7.7 months versus 6% and 3.1 months in the vorinostat arm. This led to FDA approval of this drug for refractory MF or Sézary syndrome (SS).

Alemtuzumab is monoclonal antibody targeting CD52 that is found on the surface of T-cells. In a retrospective cohort analysis, it has had response rates of 70% in patients with SS and 25% in patients with MF with evidence of long-term remission in SS but less long-term effectiveness in MF and transformed CTCL. Due to suppression of T-cells, infectious complications, especially with CMV reactivation, can be an issue.

Extracorporeal photochemotherapy (ECP) has response rates between 33% and 74% in trials of patients with erythrodermic MF. In a cohort study of 98 patients with SS treated with extracorporeal photopheresis and one or more systemic immunostimulatory agent, 73 had significant improvement with 30% having a complete response and 45% with a partial response.

For advanced CTCL, allogeneic stem-cell transplantation may be of some benefit with potential for long-term remissions. However, this is a very toxic therapy with non-relapse mortality of 20% at one year, so its use is usually limited to young patients with few comorbidities, good performance status, and high-risk CTCL. BAD guidelines (2018) recommend against autologous stem-cell transplant in patients with advanced stages of mycosis fungoides or Sezary syndrome.

Emerging evidence suggests there may now be a role for allograft in selected patients with advanced MF or SS. Between 2016-2022 a propensity score matched, controlled prospective trial allocated patients with suitable donor to allograft compared to those without donor. The median progression free survival was 9 months in the allograft arm contrasting with 3 months without allograft.

Early-stage mycosis fungoides (MF) typically has an indolent course with slow progression over years from patches to plaques, and may rarely develop tumors and involve visceral organs or lymph nodes. C
Sézary syndrome (SS) has a less favorable prognosis with median survival between 1 to 4 years.C
Of 1905 patients from Dutch and Austrian registries, patients with MF had an 88% disease-specific 5-year survival, while those with SS had a 24% disease-specific 5-year survival.B
Predictors of poorer prognosis include older age, advanced stage, and blood involvement.C

Many patients with early-stage disease will never have progression of their disease. Only 16% of patients with T1 disease (<10% skin involvement) at diagnosis will have progression at 20 years. For those with T2 disease (10% to 80% skin involvement without tumors) this number is 40%, while it is around 80% for patients with tumors (T3) or erythroderma (T4).
Patients with advanced-stage mycosis fungoides (MF) or Sézary syndrome (SS) typically die of systemic involvement or infections.

Based on a retrospective cohort study of 1798 patients, patients with MF or SS have significantly elevated risks of other diseases such as Hodgkin disease (6 cases; standardized incidence ratio (SIR) = 17.1; 95% CI, 6.3-37.3) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma (27 cases; SIR = 5.1; 95% CI, 3.3-7.4), melanoma (10 cases; SIR = 2.6; 95% CI, 1.3-4.8), and urinary cancer (21 cases; SIR = 1.7; 95% CI, 1.1-2.7). In a smaller cohort of 429 patients, there was also an elevated risk of biliary cancer (2 cases; SIR = 11.8; 95% CI, 1.5-42.0).

Based on Dutch and Austrian registries, among 1905 patients with primary cutaneous lymphoma, those with mycosis fungoides (MF) had an 88% disease-specific 5-year survival, whereas patients with Sézary syndrome (SS) had a 24% disease-specific 5-year survival. Those with lower stages of MF had higher disease-specific 5-year survival; those with stage IA had a 5-year survival of 100%.
The most significant clinical prognostic factors in a review of outcomes of 525 patients with MF and SS were patient age, T-cell classification, and the presence of extracutaneous disease.

In studies of patients with MF, the amount of skin involvement also affected disease-specific survival with 10-year disease-specific survivals of 97% to 98% for patients with limited patch/plaque disease (<10% of the skin surface), and 83% for patients with generalized patch/plaque disease (>10% of the skin surface).
In advanced-stage CTCL, prognosis is poor with median survival of around 2.9 years. In patients with SS, median survival is about 13 months.

In a cohort study of 393 patients with MF and SS in the southeastern US, 20% died of disease and 22% had disease progression. Advanced stages and older age were predictors of poor disease-specific survival but race was not.

In a study of 106 patients with MF or SS, the most important prognostic factors were age at presentation, overall stage, and peripheral blood involvement, with unfavorable prognostic factors having a median survival of 1.5 years.

MF can transform into more aggressive T-cell lymphomas, which portends a worse prognosis. Of 100 patients with large-cell transformation in MF, CD30 negativity, folliculotropic MF, extent of skin involvement, and extracutaneous transformation were associated with reduced disease-specific survival.
In patients with CD30+ lymphoproliferative disorders, spontaneous regression of tumors has been observed in up to 44% of patients.

feature.caption: Staging of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. See for definitions.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Skin (T) Node (N) Visceral (M) Blood (B)
IA 1 0 0 0-1
IB 2 0 0 0-1
IIA 1-2 1 0 0-1
IIB 3 0-2 0 0-1
IIIA 4 0-2 0 0
IIIB 4 0-2 0 1
IVA1 1-4 0-2 0 2
IVA2 1-4 3 0 0-2
IVB 1-4 0-3 1 0-2
Adapted from Olsen et al. Revisions to the staging and classification of mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome: a proposal of the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL) and the cutaneous lymphoma task force of the European Organization of Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC). Blood. 2007 Sep 15;110(6):1713–22.

feature.caption: Tumor, node, visceral, and blood staging definitions for CTCL.
feature.feature_body:
Tumor
T1 Limited patches, papules, and/or plaques covering <10% of the skin surface
T2 Patches, papules, or plaques covering ≥10% of the skin surface
T3 One or more tumors (>1 cm diameter)
T4 Confluence of erythroderma covering >80% body surface area
Node
N0 No clinically abnormal lymph nodes
N1 Clinically abnormal peripheral lymph nodes; histopathology Dutch Grade 1 or NCI LN0-2
N2 Clinically abnormal peripheral lymph nodes; histopathology Dutch Grade 2 or NCI LN3
N3 Clinically abnormal peripheral lymph nodes; histopathology Dutch Grade 3-4 or NCI LN4
Visceral
M0 No visceral organ involvement
M1 Visceral involvement (must have pathology confirmation)
Blood
B0 Absence of significant blood involvement: ≤5% of peripheral blood lymphocytes are atypical (Sézary) cells
B1 Low blood tumor burden: >5% of peripheral blood lymphocytes are atypical (Sézary) cells
B2 High blood tumor burden: ≥1000 µL Sézary cells with positive clones
Adapted from Olsen et al. Revisions to the staging and classification of mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome: a proposal of the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas (ISCL) and the cutaneous lymphoma task force of the European Organization of Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC). Blood. 2007 Sep 15;110(6):1713–22.
